item.title: Which journey should we test?
item.description:
Before we start creating tests with Synthetics, let’s look at what real users are doing to prioritize test coverage. RUM tells us which pages real end users interact with, how those pages feel, and where the experience breaks down.

Exercise · Open our store and check the Web Vitals
  • From the main menu, select Digital Experience, then Overview under Real User Monitoring.
  • Set the filters to our own store:
    • Time frame: -1h
    • Environment: [NAME OF WORKSHOP]-workshop
    • App: [NAME OF WORKSHOP]-store
    • Source: Browser
  • Select the [NAME OF WORKSHOP]-store link above the Page Views / JavaScript Errors chart to open the application view.
  • On the UX Metrics tab, find the three Core Web Vitals charts.

item.title: Build our browser test
item.description:
A browser test drives a real Google Chrome browser through a journey we script, from the locations we choose, on the schedule we set. In the Introduction module we reviewed a browser test somebody else had built. Now we build our own, for the checkout journey we just chose.

Two concepts do most of the work:

  • A step is one interaction — go to a URL, click something, or assert that something is there. Steps have names, and those names are what we read when a test fails.
  • A synthetic transaction is a named group of steps representing a business-critical flow. Each transaction gets its own duration, requests, and size metrics, which is how we end up able to say “checkout got slower” rather than just “the test got slower”.

Everyone shares one shop

item.title: Run the test and read the results
item.description:
Our test now runs every five minutes, but we do not have to wait five minutes to see results. Run now triggers a scheduled-quality run on demand.

Exercise · Trigger runs on demand
  • On our test’s page, select . We can also do this from the Synthetics test list, using the vertical dots ⋮ next to the test.
  • Trigger three or four runs, waiting for each to finish before starting the next. Because roughly half of all checkouts fail, a handful of runs gives us a mix of passes and failures to look at.
  • Runs triggered this way are labelled Manual in the results list, to distinguish them from the scheduled ones.

Note

item.title: Beat the tweet
item.description:
A test that finds a problem nobody is told about is just a nicely formatted record of an outage. The thing that actually beats social media to the issue is the detector.

In the Introduction module we previewed a detector on run duration and closed it without saving. This time we are going to activate one.

Alert on uptime, not on duration #

Run duration is a good signal for slow. For broken, we use Uptime, because the uptime metric is 0 on a failed run and 100 on a successful one. That makes it the one metric that catches every kind of failure — a timeout, a failed assertion, a certificate problem, or the site being gone entirely — without us having to predict which.

item.title: Beyond the browser test
item.description:
Browser tests prove a customer can complete a workflow, regardless of the resources and endpoints involved.

Uptime tests focus on the health of critical endpoints that are required for your end users to complete their tasks. These tests are much more lightweight and can be run much more frequently, so that while our browser tests are evaluating health of workflows, uptime tests are pinpointing health of individual pieces of those workflows.

item.title: One view, multiple perspectives
item.description:
Synthetics provides the lab perspective of user experience, while RUM provides the field perspective. While the lab is controlled and operating regardless of user traffic, the field reflects the reality of our end users - including all uncontrolled variables like activity, device version, network, geolocation, and so on.

Exercise · Read the combined dashboard
  • From the main menu, select Dashboards and open the Digital Experience — Astronomy Shop dashboard group for this workshop.
  • Work down the dashboard and answer these three questions in order:
    1. Is it available? Check the synthetic uptime and failed run count.
    2. What’s happening for end users? Check whether real user errors and checkout durations move at the same time.
    3. What is broken? Check the synthetic transaction durations to see whether browsing or checkout degraded.

Better together #

What does comparing Synthetic metrics to RUM help us understand? Here are some examples.

item.title: Wrap-up
item.description:
What we accomplished #

  1. Used RUM to choose a target — Core Web Vitals, per-page comparison, and front-end health, to pick the one journey worth monitoring around the clock
  2. Built a Synthetics browser test with named steps and two synthetic transactions covering that journey
  3. Validated and ran it on demand, and read uptime, availability, and transaction-level results
  4. Activated a detector on the uptime metric, then watched it fire on a failing checkout
  5. Added an uptime test and met the other test types, including SSL certificate tests
  6. Reviewed a combined dashboard pairing lab measurements with real customer experience

The habit worth taking away #

Our checkout test asserts that an order was confirmed, not that a button was clickable. That single design choice is what turns a monitoring setup from decorative into useful. Everything else on this page is mechanics.
